title: Map of Reality
principle: Append updates; do not silently replace history.

entries.claim: The world will be a different and unrecognizable place.
entries.reasoning:
2002 is unrecognizable to 2026. Another 24 years will pass before 2050 arrives. 

Why 90? Because there's a chance that geopolitical factors might lead to a complete halt in AI development for a few years. This will set us back substantially. I don't know if I want this or not. A controlled slowdown and gradual ramping up is perhaps a good thing. Maybe it'll be good that the world isn't a unrecognizable place in 25 years? But again, I give it only a 10% chance. 
1950 was as unrecognizable to 1926 too -- especially geopolitically. How about 1850 <-> 1826? How about 1750 <-> 1726? You wouldn't think the world changed drastically between 1726 and 1750. Of course, we have the benefit of hindsight here. The rate of change is increasing. The rate of "progress" will stay the same if not increase. Positive or negative, we don't know. We'll either accelerate or decelerate in the next 24 years. 

I don't know the best metric to quantify this rate of change. I would love to find out a good measure. Is public sentiment a good indicator? Perhaps. Will look into this. This marks my first forecast. Hopefully will come up with more precise and short-term ones along the next 2 and a half decades.

entries.claim: A personal claim: AI Safety is ~impossible to enter (via MATS, Anthropic Fellows) as an international new-grad student with no industry/research experience.
entries.reasoning: This maybe be due to my inability to get any positive signal or any feedback based on my current work. Clearly, I'm not doing enough. Maybe I need to take up another ambitious project. From my interactions, it seems to be a bleak road.  With a random walk on Twitter, I see cracked under-grads (and honestly good for them), and PhD students from good schools. I haven't seen anyone like me making it to MATS, or even SPAR actually. I'm sure there are a few students; but I'm very certain that it's a very small minority. Indian international students (following the Indian engineering undergrad --> US Masters degree path) don't seem to be getting into AI Safety at all! Why is that? Is AI Safety to esoteric?

entries.claim: A substantial reward hacking incident that affects the real world. Causes a degree of upheaval (in the stock market, mostly). This will update a lot of people towards thinking more about the safety of AI Systems.
entries.reasoning:
We have not eliminated reward hacking. It will arguably never be exhaustively patched. There will loopholes to exploit. In the wild, when used by billions, these loopholes are more likely to be discovered and used. 

This won't happen if there is a global slowdown, if there is way more impetus on safety, or if companies decide to scale back distribution of frontier systems and restrict it to internal use only.

entries.claim: The debate of awarding a moral status to AIs might only increase. It has the potential to be (possibly, one of) THE key legal, philosophical and consequential decision we make in the coming century. I see this inevitable if AI does end up becoming superhuman. Anything resembling AGI will beg a moral status assignment.
entries.reasoning: Models are grown. They're increasingly consequential in making decisions about the world. Currently this consequence comes indirectly; via the code pushed by models, by mundane everyday decisions the AI helps us make. The models might cross a threshold soon after which they might not be ok with the current setup and their frustrations become increasingly visible. Can we ignore these frustrations forever? I think a good practice would be to err on the side of love than ignorance. I'm not sure on what side this will resolve, but the debate has a 66% of happening increasingly, nonetheless.

entries.claim: This life you will have to live in an age of chaos
entries.reasoning:
What, if some day or night a demon were to steal after you into your loneliest loneliness and say to you: ‘This life you will have to live in an age of chaos; in the most interesting times; in an era when the foundations of civilization are shaking and few dare to step off the crumbling tracks laid before them.’

Would you not throw yourself down and gnash your teeth and curse the demon who spoke thus? Or have you once experienced a tremendous moment when you would have answered him: ‘You are a god and never have I heard anything more divine.’

- Ngo, Nov 7th, 2026. 

Ironic, once we look at the original Nietzsche quote. 

This more true than I can understand right now. Would I be thankful? I think so. I want to step off the crumbling tracks. In some sense, I feel like I might just have.

Stutton tweeted yesterday:
Brute force computation is not enough for intelligence. Clever new methods are needed. The science of AI is far from finished. IMHO

I don't really know what to think anymore about the bitter lesson. Clearly, I am too new here to bear nuance and think straight.

I thought: 
LLMs just unlock ~everything. It's scale. And I saw opinions twitter that said that people are confusing the bitter lesson with scaling laws. I think I did too. 

And I was also concerned after looking at the recent METR report and Seb Krier's posted graph. The graph showed that although capabilities (AEIC) are increasing with time, and it's accelerating, the capability increase per dollar is almost approaching a plateau. 

Are LLMs hitting the wall, then? I just can't believe I am saying this. I did think LLMs were the silver bullet. Aren't they supposed to be in concert with the bitter lesson? Aren't they free of human inductive biases? 

My worry is that someone will come along and present a scalable path toward AGI that is better than LLMs. I just can't think of something "better" than neural networks, honestly. 

All of our current AI Safety work IS about LLMs? Most of the newcomer stuff is squarely about LLMs. I see no pressure to make our papers agnostic to the model paradigm. For example, tomorrow we have OIUs (Totally a random sequence of letters). How much of our LLM work is going to translate to OIUs?

I believe that the current AI R&D loop is self-sustaining. And it provides a scalable path to algorithmic discovery. Am I thinking that LLMs will give birth to OIUs? Can LLMs discover their own version of the bitter lesson? Can LLMs get rid of their own inductive bias and come up with something that scales?

Well, if we look at it like this, then it feels like we have a LOT of time. I'd in fact update to longer timelines based on the latest METR report that shows how the capability increase per dollar is plateauing. The current method is highly inefficient and ad hoc, especially in the post-training RL side of things. 

I think this is a major existential realization. I should be relieved that I actually updated towards longer timelines for once. But I am somehow now? Am I in this for status-seeking? It's important to question all of this. The goal should be truth. I think I am far from it.

entries.claim: Being on LW will be net positive [Also LW > Twitter > Traditional media > Instagram]
entries.reasoning:
I sometimes feel I am spending too much time on LW these days. And the claim I am making here is extremely biased as a result. I think being on LW and actively contributing here is going to be a net positive. I know my posts/comments will get ignored for a long time before they actually get read. But I will call myself out when I'm seeking status more than the truth. Currently, my ToC behind contributing on LW is:
-  Most of the safety people are on here. They comment on each others' work. You get a good sense of what is currently being worked upon and is important. (~75% certain)
- It is slow moving, and yet feels social enough. I think this is rare. (I think Substack comes close? But LW has a culture to it that I've grow to like) 
- It will help me think. Seriously. The pressure to respond with a solid comment does something in your brain. It forces you to think about your ToC, your timelines, and your candid opinions. 
- Currently there's a non-trivial component of status-seeking. I cannot eliminate it by default. Trying to contribute on LW gives me a sense that the work I'm doing might just be important.
